enrichment.short_title: Employment tribunal bias challenge on secret recording
key_facts: Mr Kemmeni, a black sales executive, claimed unfair dismissal, breach of contract and race discrimination against his employer and two individuals.
An employment tribunal dismissed all claims, finding he had terminated his own employment by submitting an IT1 and had secretly recorded meetings.
The tribunal suspected he was secretly recording the hearing itself and required all parties to surrender mobile phones.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal allowed two grounds to proceed but refused permission on the alleged bias ground and other matters.
On renewed application to the Court of Appeal, Kemmeni appeared in person arguing the EAT should have allowed the bias allegation to a full hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision at a preliminary hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; no real prospect of success on bias or remaining grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Suspicion that a litigant may have been secretly recording proceedings, leading the tribunal to require surrender of electronic devices, does not on the Porter v Magill test indicate a real possibility of bias when determining substantive claims; the EAT was entitled to conclude no further investigation was necessary.
legal_issues: Whether the EAT should have allowed an allegation of employment tribunal bias to proceed
Application of the fair-minded observer test for apparent bias
Whether the EAT failed by not obtaining notes of evidence
Whether the tribunal was obliged to refer expressly to the written contract on a Boo.com commission issue

enrichment.short_title: Crown Court sentencing powers after magistrates committal
key_facts: Whitehead pleaded guilty to nine offences including theft, handling, possessing a bladed article, absconding and common assault, receiving a total of 30 months.
The memorandum of conviction recorded some either-way offences as committed under section 4 of the 2000 Act, but no related offence had been committed for trial so section 4 was unavailable.
Offences committed under section 6 were subject to magistrates' sentencing limits in the Crown Court.
The nine-month sentence for possessing a bladed article exceeded the six-month single-offence limit and was unlawful.
The aggregate of summary and either-way sentences committed under section 6 also exceeded permitted limits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for leave to appeal against sentence referred to the full Court of Appeal by the Registrar.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted; appeal succeeded only to the extent of correcting unlawful sentences while preserving a 30-month total through adjustments to section 3 committals.
enrichment.ratio: Where magistrates' purported section 4 committal is a misrecording and section 3 would have conferred power, the Crown Court may treat the committal as lawful; for valid section 6 committals the Crown Court's powers are confined to those of magistrates, and unlawful individual or aggregate sentences must be quashed and adjusted.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates validly committed either-way offences for sentence
Construction of section 4 versus section 3 of the 2000 Act
Whether Crown Court sentencing limits were exceeded for section 6 committals
Whether the overall 30-month sentence was manifestly excessive

enrichment.short_title: Disclosure of police caution interviews in prisoner assault claims
key_facts: Prisoners at Wormwood Scrubs brought civil claims against the Home Office alleging assault by prison officers.
Police interviewed suspect prison officers under caution during a criminal investigation; some officers were prosecuted but not in these cases.
Claimants sought third-party disclosure of interview transcripts from the Commissioner of Police under CPR 31.17.
Judge Collins ordered disclosure with strict conditions limiting use; prison officers appealed on principle.
Officers argued confidentiality of caution interviews should generally prevent disclosure in subsequent civil proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against county court orders for third-party disclosure in parallel civil claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; disclosure ordered subject to stringent conditions preserving confidentiality as far as possible.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 31.17, where interview records are likely relevant and disclosure is necessary for a fair disposal, the court must balance the public interest in confidentiality of police interviews against the public interest in civil trials on full evidence; interviews under caution are not a special category immune from disclosure, and stringent use conditions may maintain confidence while permitting disclosure.
legal_issues: Construction of CPR 31.17(3)(a) and (b) on third-party disclosure
Whether police interviews under caution are confidential and protected from civil disclosure
Balancing competing public interests in confidentiality and fair trial
Whether Kennedy LJ's 'exceptional circumstances' language in Woolgar creates a general bar

enrichment.short_title: Subrogation between negligent certifier and unjustly enriched bank

statutes_considered.title: Law Reform (Married Women and Tortfeasors) Act 1935

key_facts: Niru paid about US$5.8 million under a letter of credit after SGS negligently issued a false inspection certificate and documents were presented.
CAI received and paid away the funds to Nikam; Niru recovered against both SGS in tort and CAI in restitution.
SGS satisfied the full judgment; CAI paid nothing.
Part 20 proceedings concerned whether SGS could recover contribution or indemnity from CAI.
Royal Brompton Hospital held restitutionary and tort claims are not the same damage for section 1 of the 1978 Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further hearing in Part 20 contribution proceedings following the main commercial fraud judgment and House of Lords authority.
enrichment.outcome: SGS entitled to subrogation against CAI for the full judgment on the claim and half the costs; no contribution under the 1978 Act or by recoupment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tortfeasor satisfies a joint judgment relieving a defendant liable only in restitution, equitable subrogation may reverse unjust enrichment at the tortfeasor's expense; a restitutionary claim to recover mistaken payment is not a claim for the same damage within the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978, and Merryweather v Nixan does not preclude subrogation except where public policy bars relief for conscious wrongdoing.
legal_issues: Whether contribution is available under the 1978 Act between tort and restitution defendants
Availability of equitable subrogation after satisfaction of a joint judgment
Whether recoupment or common law contribution provides an alternative remedy
Effect of CAI having parted with the enriched funds

enrichment.short_title: Remitter on corporation tax postponement application
key_facts: Pumahaven participated in a 1996 tax avoidance scheme involving property lettings, asset sale and loan relationships, receiving about £112 million rent.
The Revenue assessed over £36 million corporation tax; Pumahaven sought postponement of payment pending appeal.
The Special Commissioner refused postponement, addressing the loan relationships argument but not the 'source' argument.
Park J set aside that decision and remitted to another Special Commissioner to consider the source argument.
The Revenue appealed only against the remitter, contending the High Court should have decided the source point itself.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by the Revenue with permission against the High Court's decision to remit a tax postponement application rather than determine the underlying legal point.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; remitter was a proper exercise of discretion.
enrichment.ratio: On a postponement application under section 55(6), Parliament entrusted to the Special Commissioners the evaluation of whether there are reasonable grounds for believing the taxpayer is overcharged; where the Commissioner failed to address a substantial argument, section 56A(4) permits remission for that evaluation and an appellate court should not usurp the Commissioners' function unless the argument is palpable nonsense.
legal_issues: Whether the High Court should decide the source argument rather than remit
Distinction between appellate and supervisory jurisdiction on tax appeals
Construction of 'it appears to the Commissioners' in sections 55(6) and 50(6)
Whether postponement applications involve pure issues of law or evaluation

enrichment.short_title: Res gestae hearsay when witness available but untruthful
key_facts: W was indicted for causing or inflicting grievous bodily harm on his mother Mrs W.
Mrs W made spontaneous res gestae statements to neighbours identifying W as her assailant but later refused to give evidence and denied the allegations on oath.
The prosecution did not call Mrs W, believing she would give untruthful exculpatory evidence.
The trial judge ruled res gestae hearsay inadmissible because Mrs W was available to give evidence.
The prosecution offered no evidence and not guilty verdicts were entered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference following acquittal on a point of law on res gestae admissibility.
enrichment.outcome: Same practical result upheld; res gestae evidence was admissible but exclusion under section 78 PACE might have been appropriate if the Crown sought to adduce it without tendering the witness.
enrichment.ratio: There is no legal bar to res gestae hearsay merely because the declarant is available; Lord Ackner's deprecation in Andrews addresses improper avoidance of calling a witness, not admissibility. Where the Crown relies on part of a witness's account without tendering her for cross-examination, the judge should consider exclusion under section 78 for unfairness rather than holding the evidence inadmissible ab initio.
legal_issues: Whether res gestae is excluded when the maker can attend but may not testify truthfully
Whether a 'best evidence' rule applies to res gestae statements
Correct procedure when prosecution declines to call an available witness
Compatibility with Article 6 ECHR

enrichment.short_title: Greek medical specialist seeking UK dermatology registration
key_facts: Dr Lambiris, a dual Greek and British national, qualified as a dermatology-venereology specialist in Greece based largely on UK hospital posts.
Dermatology-venereology is not a UK-listed specialty; he sought entry on the UK specialist register as a dermatologist under article 9(3) of the ESMQO.
The Specialist Training Authority rejected his application, finding his UK posts were not recognised supervised training posts under Article 24 of the Directive.
Greek certification of his UK experience did not bind the host state where training occurred in the United Kingdom.
Rix LJ dissented, arguing the STA should have determined his rights under Article 8 of the Directive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against dismissal of judicial review of the Specialist Training Authority appeal panel decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a host Member State assesses specialist training undertaken in its own territory, it may verify content and duration against its own requirements and is not bound by another Member State's certificate; article 9(3) of the ESMQO requires assessment of whether a foreign qualification gives NHS consultant-level knowledge and skill, which legitimately focuses on supervised training in recognised posts rather than a separate skills examination.
legal_issues: Construction of Article 8 and Article 9(3) of the ESMQO and Directive 93/16
Whether the STA could go behind the Greek specialist certificate
Whether Article 8 required identification of a training gap
Whether Community law permitted recognition without UK-approved training posts

enrichment.short_title: Asylum credibility challenge by Nepalese Maoist claimant
key_facts: Mr Gautam, a Nepalese national, claimed asylum based on membership of the Maoist party and alleged arrest, detention and torture.
He arrived on a false passport, did not claim asylum immediately, and was arrested two days later during a raid.
The adjudicator found his evidence not credible, doubting arrest and detention partly because he was released and because post-release Maoist activity was 'bizarre'.
Fresh evidence showed Maoist campaigns against alcohol consumption in rural areas.
Dr Shehadeh's report diagnosed PTSD linked to alleged detention and torture, but the adjudicator did not properly weigh it.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an immigration adjudicator's decision dismissing asylum and human rights appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Adjudicator's decision quashed; matter remitted to a differently constituted adjudicator.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator's adverse credibility findings on detention and torture must be rationally supported; reasons such as disbelief because authorities released the claimant or because anti-alcohol activity seemed unrelated to Maoism are inadequate, and a psychiatric report attributing PTSD to alleged torture must be weighed rather than summarily dismissed where the factual account is not wholly discredited.
legal_issues: Rationality of credibility findings on Maoist membership and detention
Whether delay in claiming asylum undermined credibility
Admissibility and weight of fresh country evidence on Maoist policies
Proper treatment of medical evidence on torture and PTSD

confidence.notes: Focused judicial review with identified irrationality in paragraph 27 and inadequate treatment of medical evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Anthony Martin parole refusal judicial review
key_facts: Anthony Martin shot and killed burglar Freddie Barras and wounded Brendon Fearon at his Norfolk farmhouse in August 1999.
He was initially convicted of murder and sentenced to life; the Court of Appeal substituted manslaughter on diminished responsibility with five years' imprisonment.
The Parole Board refused parole in January 2003, citing risk of further reactive violence and lack of remorse.
The parole dossier omitted the Court of Appeal judgment and psychiatric reports of Dr Joseph and Miss Craissati.
After challenge, panel members reviewed the missing material and maintained the refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Rolled-up judicial review application challenging Parole Board refusal of parole and refusal to reconsider.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted on ground 1 only; no quashing order; parole refusal upheld; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: The Parole Board erred initially in deciding parole without the Court of Appeal judgment and pre-sentence psychiatric reports where the offence had become manslaughter on diminished responsibility, but that error was remedied by later consideration and would not have changed the outcome; a prisoner's continuing belief that shooting burglars was justified may legitimately weigh heavily on future risk despite Zulfikar principles on denial of guilt.
legal_issues: Whether the Parole Board failed to consider mandatory material on changed conviction and sentence
Whether risk assessment was irrational
Application of Zulfikar to lack of remorse and offence-focused work
Effect of media interest on parole decision

enrichment.short_title: Algerian army deserter Article 3 return challenge
key_facts: Mr Mouhoub, an Algerian conscript, deserted his army unit in August 1999 after a traumatic military exercise.
He claimed a real risk of Article 3 ill-treatment if returned as a deserter.
Expert evidence agreed he faced imprisonment of between six months and ten years for wartime desertion within Algeria.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal preferred CIPU country information over Mr Joffé's report and found no real risk of torture in detention.
The tribunal used 'reasonable likelihood' language rather than the preferred 'real risk' formulation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision dismissing a human rights claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; proposed amendment on 10–20 year desertion abroad penalty refused.
enrichment.ratio: On Article 3 expulsion cases the correct test is whether the claimant faces a real risk of proscribed treatment, assessing both seriousness and likelihood; even if a tribunal misstates the test as reasonable likelihood, the court will not interfere where the evaluative conclusion on country evidence would inevitably be the same.
legal_issues: Correct Article 3 threshold: real risk versus reasonable likelihood
Whether Algerian deserters face Article 3 treatment on return
Appropriate penalty scale for desertion within Algeria in wartime
Appellate review of tribunal evaluation of country evidence
